fields.title: Litera: fewer than half reach the second lesson
fields.summary: Students drop off after the first lesson. Reviews, metrics, and a ready survey say different things. Decide where to start.
fields.decisionPrompt: What will you do in these four days?
fields.brief/role: You are the product manager for the "First Lesson" track at Litera.
fields.brief/company: Litera is a fictional tutor matching service. A student submits a request, the service matches a tutor, and the first lesson is trial and free.
fields.brief/context: The share of students reaching the second (paid) lesson fell from 58% to 44% over six months. The head of product assembled the team and asked for a hypothesis by Thursday. You have 340 store reviews for the quarter, an analyst summary, and a ready survey that marketing wants to send to everyone who didn't reach the second lesson.
fields.brief/objective: Find the mechanism causing students to drop off before the second lesson.
fields.brief/constraints: Four days. The analyst is available for half a day. The survey is formatted and can go out tomorrow; after sending, you won't be able to survey the same people again.
fields.brief/task: Decide what to do in these four days and justify why.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: Look for concentration before looking for cause
fields.learnTakeaway/body: When an aggregate metric drops, the first move is not collecting new data, but segmenting existing data. If the drop is concentrated in a single segment, segmentation rules out all explanations that would shift the entire base — and does so in hours. A qualitative study after that answers "why here," rather than "where to look at all."
fields.evidenceCards/0/content:
340 reviews, average rating 4.1.

Among reviews rated 1–3 (71 total), the most repeated words are: "expensive" — 22 times, "didn't fit" — 19, "took too long" — 17.

Reading through them shows that "didn't fit" refers both to tutors and schedules ("time didn't fit"). "Took too long" refers to both matching wait times and lesson duration.

Separately: 9 reviews were written by parents, not students, and all nine mention that "it was unclear what happened in the lesson."
fields.evidenceCards/1/content:
Over the last 90 days:
- Requests: 12,400
- Matched: 81%
- First lesson held: 63%
- Second lesson paid: 44% of those who had a first lesson

Average time from request to first lesson: 2.6 days.
Average student rating for first lesson: 4.6 out of 5.

Analyst note: "These are averages across all requests. I haven't done segmentations by subject, age, or acquisition channel — tell me what you need, and I'll do it in a couple of hours. Only 38% of students rate the lesson; the rest skip the screen."
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
Blast email to everyone who didn't reach the second lesson this quarter (about 4,300 people). Questions:

1. How much did you enjoy the trial lesson? (1–5)
2. Do you plan to continue lessons in the future?
3. What is usually more important when choosing a tutor: price, experience, or schedule?
4. Would you take lessons if we offered a discount on the first month?

Marketing comment: "We want to send it tomorrow before the quarter ends. We won't contact these people again — this is our only shot."
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
The matching team keeps a manual spreadsheet.

Over the quarter, there were 1,100 cases where a student requested a different tutor after the first lesson. 640 of those were in "math, grades 9–11," even though this subject accounts for only 22% of all requests.

Matching lead: "We've seen this for a while. We lack strong tutors for high school math, so we assign whoever is available. I brought this up at the team meeting in May."

Customer acquisition cost is 640 ₽. A paid second lesson breaks even on acquisition in about three lessons.
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: Segment the funnel by subject and break down reviews; hold the survey
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Spend the analyst's half-day on segmentations by subject, age, and channel. Categorize reviews by what users actually talk about. Hold off on the survey until it's clear what to ask.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
Segmentations are ready in three hours. For 9–11th grade math, the share reaching the second lesson is 27%; for other subjects, it is 51%. A single subject representing 22% of requests accounts for almost the entire drop.
Review analysis confirms: "didn't fit" in negative reviews is more often about tutors than schedules, concentrated in that same segment. The average lesson rating of 4.6 turns out useless — only 38% rate it, and those who left rarely do.
The survey is rewritten for one segment with a single question about past behavior: "tell us what happened after the trial lesson." It goes out a week later and gets a 12% response rate instead of the usual 4%.
By Thursday, the team has the mechanism: a shortage of strong tutors in one subject, which ops reported in May.
Trade-off: you delayed the mailing and used half a day of analyst time that could have been spent calculating something else.
fields.decisionOptions/1/label: Send the survey tomorrow as is
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: 4,300 people is the largest reachable sample, and there won't be a second chance. Send it and work with the results.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
The survey goes out, 4% answer (172 people). 61% choose "price" in question 3, 58% reply they would continue with a discount.
The team offers a discount on the first month. A quarter later, the share reaching the second lesson is 46%, while revenue per student drops.
During post-mortem, someone notices question 3 asked what is "usually" important, question 4 offered a leading solution, and the 9–11th grade math segment wasn't isolated.
These people cannot be surveyed again.
Trade-off: you wasted your single outreach to 4,300 people on questions that couldn't disprove anything.
fields.decisionOptions/2/label: Tackle the shortage of math tutors
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: Operations already stated the cause in May: a shortage of strong tutors in high school math. Start recruiting without wasting four days on analysis.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
Recruiting starts immediately. Two months later, 40 tutors are added for 9–11th grade math, and the second-lesson rate in this segment rises from 27% to 43%.
This is a real improvement from a source no one checked with numbers. But the overall rate increases only to 47% because nobody measured the segment size in advance, and the head of product asks where the expected impact figure came from.
The survey goes out unchanged, producing the same useless 4%.
Trade-off: you trusted the right source but couldn't show what share of the problem it explained.
fields.decisionOptions/3/label: Conduct eight interviews with dropped-off students
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: Use the four days to talk to eight people who didn't reach the second lesson and understand the cause directly.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
You manage to reach five people in four days; two are parents. Conversations are useful: three describe how the tutor "didn't explain, just re-read the textbook," two couldn't agree on scheduling.
This points in the right direction, but five people without segmentation fail to show that the issue is concentrated in one segment, whereas the ops table showed that for free.
By Thursday, the team has a plausible narrative but no measure of problem size.
Trade-off: you pursued qualitative explanations, spending your entire window, even though the quantitative answer was sitting in two tables.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: Feedback was not categorized by what the user was trying to do
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: Volume of noise was mistaken for problem severity
fields.rubric/remediation/2/gap: An average was taken as a description of user behavior
fields.rubric/remediation/3/gap: A metric was named without a goal or an observable signal
fields.rubric/remediation/4/gap: Interview questions ask about the future or about "usually"
fields.rubric/remediation/5/gap: Research was planned without a falsifiable hypothesis
fields.rubric/remediation/6/gap: A customer's feature request was mistaken for their underlying problem
